questions.stem: A 37 year old man attends a workplace health check. He weighs 96 kg and is 1.80 m tall. He has no symptoms and takes no medication. His BP is 132/82 mmHg. His HbA1c and lipids are normal. He asks how his weight is classified.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate classification of his weight?
questions.e: BMI = 96 ÷ 1.8² ≈ 29.6 kg/m², which falls in the overweight band of 25 to 29.9.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate classification of his weight? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

elim: Healthy BMI is 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m²; his is about 29.6.
Obesity starts at BMI 30 kg/m².
Severe obesity is BMI 40 kg/m² or more.
Underweight is BMI below 18.5 kg/m².

steps.x: C. Overweight. Overweight 25–29.9, obesity ≥30, severe obesity ≥40 kg/m².

questions.stem: A 55 year old lorry driver with a BMI of 41 kg/m² has fallen asleep at traffic lights twice this month. His partner says he snores and stops breathing at night. He wakes with headaches. His collar size is 19 inches. His BP is 152/94 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Obesity causes OSA by upper airway fat deposition: snoring, witnessed apnoeas, morning headache and daytime sleepiness.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Large neck, loud snoring, apnoeas and daytime sleepiness in severe obesity.

elim: Causes breathlessness and cough, not witnessed apnoeas.
Can cause sleepiness but not witnessed apnoeas and loud snoring.
Sleep attacks with cataplexy, usually in young people, without snoring.
Causes daytime hypercapnia and low saturations; his saturation is normal.

steps.x: E. Obstructive sleep apnoea. Obesity → upper airway fat → OSA.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman with a BMI of 37 kg/m² has 4 months of burning retrosternal pain after large meals and when bending forward. She has an acid taste in her mouth at night. She has no dysphagia, weight loss or vomiting. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Obesity raises intra-abdominal pressure, causing reflux; burning pain after meals and when bending plus acid brash is GORD.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Postural, meal-related burning with acid brash and no red flags.

elim: Causes progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids.
Right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, not retrosternal burning.
Expect dysphagia and weight loss; she has neither.
Brought on by exertion, not meals or bending.

steps.x: C. Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Obesity → raised intra-abdominal pressure → GORD (and Barrett's).

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with a BMI of 39 kg/m² has had reflux symptoms for 20 years treated with antacids. Endoscopy shows salmon-pink mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction. Biopsy shows columnar epithelium with goblet cells.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding?
questions.e: Long-standing reflux from obesity causes metaplasia to columnar epithelium with goblet cells: Barrett's oesophagus.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Chronic reflux, salmon-pink mucosa, intestinal metaplasia.

elim: White plaques, usually in immunosuppression.
Rings and furrows with eosinophils on biopsy, often in young atopic men.
A mucosal tear after vomiting with haematemesis.
Dilated veins from portal hypertension.

steps.x: A. Barrett's oesophagus. Obesity → GORD → Barrett's oesophagus.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman with a BMI of 35 kg/m² has routine bloods before starting a weight management programme. She drinks 4 units of alcohol a week. She has no symptoms. Her BP is 128/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her abnormal liver tests?
questions.e: Mild ALT rise in an obese woman with low alcohol intake and insulin resistance is NAFLD, a complication of obesity.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her abnormal liver tests? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Obesity, minimal alcohol, mild hepatitic picture.

elim: She drinks only 4 units a week.
Usually much higher transaminases and raised IgG.
Expect a raised transferrin saturation; ferritin alone is mildly raised in fatty liver.
Gives a cholestatic picture with raised ALP.

steps.x: D. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Obesity complications include NAFLD; baseline LFTs are part of the work-up.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man with a BMI of 33 kg/m² and a waist circumference of 108 cm has baseline bloods. He has no thirst or polyuria. His BP is 138/86 mmHg. Investigations: HbA1c 44 mmol/mol (<42), total cholesterol 5.9 mmol/L (<5.0), triglycerides 2.3 mmol/L (<1.7).
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of his HbA1c?
questions.e: HbA1c 42 to 47 mmol/mol is pre-diabetes, a recognised complication of obesity along with dyslipidaemia.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely interpretation of his HbA1c? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
HbA1c between 42 and 47.

elim: Needs very high glucose, ketones and acidosis.
HbA1c below 42 mmol/mol is normal.
Presents with weight loss, thirst and ketones, not this.
Diagnosed at HbA1c 48 mmol/mol or more.

steps.x: C. Pre-diabetes. Obesity → pre-diabetes, T2DM, dyslipidaemia, hypertension.

questions.stem: A 10 year old girl is referred for obesity. Over a year she has gained weight mainly around her face and trunk, and her growth has slowed: her height has fallen from the 50th to the 9th centile. She has purple abdominal striae. Her BP is 128/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her obesity?
questions.e: Weight gain with falling height velocity, purple striae and hypertension suggest Cushing's syndrome as an underlying cause.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her obesity? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: height has fallen from the 50th to the 9th centile
steps.x: Obese child who is getting shorter relative to peers: endocrine cause.

elim: Recognised at birth with characteristic facies and learning disability.
Neonatal hypotonia and hyperphagia from infancy.
Children with dietary obesity are usually tall for their age, not slowing in height.
Short stature but not truncal obesity, striae and hypertension.

steps.x: A. Cushing's syndrome. Childhood obesity causes: Down, hypothyroidism, Cushing's, Prader-Willi.

questions.stem: A 12 year old boy has gained 8 kg in a year. He is tired, constipated and feels the cold. His teacher says his school work has deteriorated. His height velocity has slowed. His pulse rate is 58 bpm. His skin is dry and his ankle reflexes are slow to relax.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his weight gain?
questions.e: Weight gain with cold intolerance, constipation, bradycardia, slowed growth and slow-relaxing reflexes is hypothyroidism.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his weight gain? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Classic hypothyroid features in an obese child.

elim: Expect striae and hypertension rather than cold intolerance and bradycardia.
Causes tall stature, not slowed growth.
Presents from infancy with hypotonia and hyperphagia.
Causes weight loss, not gain.

steps.x: C. Hypothyroidism. Look for an underlying cause in childhood obesity.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman weighs 128 kg and is 1.62 m tall. She has become breathless walking to the shops and now uses a stick because of knee pain. She has no chest pain or cough. Her chest is clear and there is no ankle oedema. Her ECG and chest X-ray are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her breathlessness?
questions.e: BMI ≈ 48.8 kg/m² (severe obesity); obesity can present with breathlessness and reduced mobility.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her breathlessness? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
BMI 128 ÷ 2.62 ≈ 49: severe obesity with a normal heart and lungs.

elim: No wheeze, cough or variability; the chest is clear.
No oedema and a normal chest X-ray.
Gradual rather than sudden, with no pleuritic pain.
Expect crackles and an abnormal chest X-ray.

steps.x: E. Severe obesity. Obesity may present with breathlessness and reduced mobility.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man works long shifts as a taxi driver. He eats takeaway meals most days and does no exercise. Both his parents are obese. His BMI has risen from 26 to 33 kg/m² over 4 years. His TSH, cortisol and HbA1c are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his weight gain?
o: Positive energy balance from diet and inactivity
questions.e: Intake persistently exceeding expenditure (poor diet, inactivity, genetic tendency) expands adipose tissue.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his weight gain? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Diet, inactivity, family history; endocrine causes excluded.

elim: Cortisol is normal.
TSH is normal.
Causes hypoglycaemic episodes; none described.
Presents in infancy with hypotonia and learning difficulty.

steps.x: D. Positive energy balance from diet and inactivity. Obesity = chronic positive energy balance.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman with a BMI of 34 kg/m² attends for a cervical smear. She has no symptoms and does not feel her weight affects her. Her BP is 134/84 mmHg. She does not smoke.
questions.q: Which best describes how obesity most often presents?
questions.e: Obesity is often asymptomatic and is picked up when weight and BMI are measured opportunistically.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best describes how obesity most often presents? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: does not feel her weight affects her
steps.x: Asymptomatic, found incidentally.

elim: Not a usual presenting feature of obesity.
That suggests ischaemic heart disease, a complication.
Suggests upper GI bleeding, not obesity itself.
Red flags for malignancy or TB.

steps.x: B. Asymptomatic, found at routine checks. Obesity is often asymptomatic; measure BMI opportunistically.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with a BMI of 38 kg/m² and a waist of 118 cm has 2 months of central chest tightness on climbing stairs, relieved by rest. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 148/90 mmHg. His resting ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Obesity drives type 2 diabetes, hypertension and dyslipidaemia, leading to cardiovascular disease such as angina.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Exertional chest pain relieved by rest in an obese man with metabolic complications.

elim: Expect an ejection systolic murmur and syncope.
Reproducible chest wall tenderness, not exertional.
Related to meals and lying, not exertion.
Breathlessness with signs of right heart strain.

steps.x: E. Stable angina. Obesity → cardiovascular disease.

questions.stem: A 5 year old boy is reviewed for obesity. He has a flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures, a single palmar crease and moderate learning difficulty. He had a heart defect repaired as a baby. His TSH is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying condition?
questions.e: Down syndrome is associated with childhood obesity; its features include flat face, upslanting fissures, single palmar crease and congenital heart disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying condition? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Dysmorphic features plus cardiac defect.

elim: Causes striae and hypertension, not dysmorphic features from birth.
Long face and large ears, not upslanting eyes and single crease.
TSH is normal.
Almond-shaped eyes, hypotonia and hyperphagia, not upslanting fissures and heart defect.

steps.x: B. Down syndrome. Childhood obesity: think Down syndrome, hypothyroidism, Cushing's, Prader-Willi.

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy is brought by his father, who thinks he is overweight compared with his classmates. He weighs 34 kg and is 1.24 m tall. He is active and has no symptoms. There are no dysmorphic features.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate method to assess whether he is obese?
o: BMI percentile for age and sex
questions.e: In children, obesity is assessed with BMI plotted on a centile chart adjusted for age and sex.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate method to assess whether he is obese? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A child: adult BMI bands do not apply.

elim: Adult thresholds do not apply in children.
Not routine for diagnosis.
Not the standard method.
The 94/80 cm cut-offs are for adults.

steps.x: B. BMI percentile for age and sex. Paediatrics: BMI percentile adjusted for age and sex.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has a BMI of 28 kg/m² and feels her weight is not a problem. She has no medical history. Her BP is 130/80 mmHg. Her GP wants a simple measurement to assess whether her fat distribution raises her cardiovascular risk.
questions.q: Above which waist circumference is her cardiovascular risk increased?
questions.e: Waist circumference above 94 cm in men and 80 cm in women indicates increased cardiovascular risk.

steps.x: The question asks: Above which waist circumference is her cardiovascular risk increased? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
She is a woman.

elim: An older very-high-risk threshold for men.
A higher cut-off from older guidance; increased risk in women starts above 80 cm.
The threshold for men.
Far above the threshold.

steps.x: C. 80 cm. Waist >94 cm men, >80 cm women.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man with a BMI of 36 kg/m² is referred to a weight management service. He has no known medical problems. His waist circumference is 115 cm. The clinic wants baseline tests to look for metabolic complications before starting treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate set of baseline investigations?
o: HbA1c, lipid profile, LFTs and blood pressure
questions.e: Baseline HbA1c, lipids, LFTs and BP screen for diabetes, dyslipidaemia, NAFLD and hypertension.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate set of baseline investigations? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: baseline tests to look for metabolic complications
steps.x: Screen for the common complications.

elim: Not a routine baseline test in obesity.
Only if Cushing's is suspected clinically.
Not measured clinically.
Only if OSA symptoms are present.

steps.x: B. HbA1c, lipid profile, LFTs and blood pressure. Baseline: HbA1c, lipids, LFTs, BP.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman attends her booking appointment at 11 weeks of gestation. Her BMI is 33 kg/m². She has no previous gestational diabetes and no family history of diabetes. Her BP is 118/74 mmHg and urine dipstick is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation for gestational diabetes?
questions.e: BMI ≥30 in pregnancy is an indication for a 75 g 2-hour OGTT at 24–28 weeks.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation for gestational diabetes? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Obese pregnant woman, no prior GDM.

elim: HbA1c is not used to diagnose gestational diabetes.
Early OGTT is for previous gestational diabetes.
Not the screening test.
Glycosuria is common in pregnancy and unreliable.

steps.x: A. 75 g 2-hour OGTT at 24–28 weeks. BMI ≥30 → OGTT at 24–28 weeks.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man with a BMI of 42 kg/m² has been on a weight management programme for a year. He snores loudly and his wife reports pauses in breathing. He falls asleep while watching TV. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 15.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Obesity follow-up includes complication screening; suspected OSA is confirmed with a sleep study.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Symptoms of OSA.

elim: Not indicated for sleepiness without neurology.
Not the diagnostic test for OSA.
Used for epilepsy, not sleep apnoea.
Assesses airway obstruction when awake, not apnoeas at night.

steps.x: D. Sleep study (polysomnography). Screen for complications: CVD, T2DM, OSA, NAFLD.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman asks her GP whether she is obese. She weighs 92 kg and is 1.70 m tall. She is not muscular and does little exercise. She has no symptoms. Her BP is 128/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm obesity?
questions.e: In adults, obesity is confirmed using BMI with clinical assessment; here BMI ≈ 31.8.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm obesity? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
BMI 92 ÷ 2.89 ≈ 31.8; not muscular, so BMI is valid.

elim: Not the standard method for diagnosis.
Accurate but not used routinely.
Not used to define obesity.
Ignores height, so cannot classify obesity.

steps.x: B. BMI with clinical assessment. Adults: BMI + clinical assessment.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has a BMI of 32 kg/m². She has no hypertension, diabetes or other weight-related conditions. She asks for help losing weight. Her BP is 124/76 mmHg and her HbA1c is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Lifestyle is first-line; adults without weight-related conditions are offered a behavioural weight management programme.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: no hypertension, diabetes or other weight-related conditions
steps.x: Obese without comorbidities.

elim: Requires BMI >40, or >35 with comorbidities.
Considered after lifestyle failure.
For BMI >35, or >30 with comorbidities.
For BMI >35 with comorbidities or >40.

steps.x: B. Behavioural weight management programme. Lifestyle first; behavioural programme.

questions.stem: A 9 year old boy has a BMI above the 98th centile. His parents are also obese. He has no dysmorphic features, his growth is normal and his TFTs are normal. He spends 5 hours a day on screens.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Very low calorie diet for the child alone
questions.e: Paediatric obesity is managed first-line with family-involved lifestyle interventions.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Child, family obesity.

elim: Not first-line in children; lifestyle comes first.
Drug treatment is not first-line in children.
Drug treatment is not first-line in children.
Unsafe for growth and ignores the family environment.

steps.x: B. Family-based lifestyle intervention. Paediatric: family-based lifestyle.

questions.stem: A 51 year old woman with a BMI of 29 kg/m² and hypertension has followed a diet and exercise plan for 6 months with little effect. She has no diabetes. Her BP is 136/84 mmHg on amlodipine.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Orlistat is offered for BMI >28 with comorbidities after lifestyle failure.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step in management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
BMI ≥27/28 with comorbidity, lifestyle failed.

elim: BMI is far below surgical thresholds.
Six months of lifestyle change has failed and she meets drug criteria.
Needs BMI >35, or >30 with comorbidities.
BMI >35 with comorbidities.

steps.x: C. Orlistat. Orlistat: BMI >28 with comorbidities.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man with a BMI of 37 kg/m² and type 2 diabetes for 12 years has not lost weight despite 1 year of lifestyle changes. He takes metformin. His HbA1c is 64 mmol/mol.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next drug?
questions.e: GLP-1 mimetics are used for BMI >35, or >30 with comorbidities such as T2DM.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next drug? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: BMI of 37 kg/m² and type 2 diabetes
steps.x: BMI >35 with T2DM.

elim: A sulfonylurea that causes weight gain.
Causes weight gain; not needed at this HbA1c first.
Less effective; GLP-1 mimetic fits BMI >35 with T2DM.
Causes weight gain and fluid retention.

steps.x: E. Semaglutide. GLP-1 mimetics: BMI >35 or >30 with comorbidities.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman started liraglutide for weight loss 6 weeks ago. She has 1 day of severe epigastric pain radiating to her back and vomiting. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Investigations: amylase 1,150 U/L (<100).
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
o: Stop liraglutide and treat acute pancreatitis
questions.e: Pancreatitis is a recognised side effect of GLP-1 mimetics; stop the drug.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
GLP-1 mimetic, epigastric pain to the back, high amylase.

elim: Does not address the acute illness.
The drug is the likely cause and must be stopped.
Would worsen the pancreatitis.
Treats as dyspepsia and misses pancreatitis with amylase over 3 times normal.

steps.x: E. Stop liraglutide and treat acute pancreatitis. GLP-1 side effect: pancreatitis.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man with a BMI of 38 kg/m² and hypertension started semaglutide. He has been on the maximum dose for 12 weeks and his weight has fallen from 120 kg to 117 kg. He has no side effects.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
questions.e: GLP-1 mimetics are stopped if less than 5% of initial weight is lost after 12 weeks at maximum dose; he lost 2.5%.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

elim: Adding a second drug does not address the GLP-1 stopping rule.
He has lost under 5%, so continuing is not cost-effective.
He is already on the maximum dose.
BMI 38 with hypertension needs Tier 3 assessment first.

steps.x: D. Stop semaglutide. Stop GLP-1 if <5% loss.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman with a BMI of 37 kg/m² has hypertension and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with CPAP. She has completed a 12 month behavioural weight management programme but her weight is unchanged. She does not have diabetes. Her BP is 142/88 mmHg on two drugs.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Refer to a Tier 3 specialist weight management service
questions.e: BMI >35 with comorbidities (or >40 without) warrants referral to a Tier 3 specialist weight management service.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
BMI above 35 plus two weight-related comorbidities, and lifestyle failed.

elim: Surgery follows assessment in a specialist (Tier 3) service.
It has already failed for a year.
Leaves severe obesity with comorbidities untreated.
She meets criteria for specialist care; orlistat alone is not enough.

steps.x: E. Refer to a Tier 3 specialist weight management service. Tier 3: BMI >35 with comorbidities or >40 without.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man with a BMI of 38 kg/m² was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 3 years ago. He has engaged fully with a Tier 3 weight management service for 2 years without sustained weight loss. He is fit for anaesthesia and committed to long-term follow-up. His HbA1c is 66 mmol/mol on metformin.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Bariatric surgery is offered for BMI >35 with recent-onset type 2 diabetes (under 10 years) after non-surgical measures fail.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
BMI over 35, diabetes under 10 years, specialist care has failed.

elim: Causes weight gain and does not treat obesity.
Causes weight gain and fluid retention.
Two years have failed; he meets surgical criteria.
Unlikely to achieve meaningful loss at this BMI after specialist failure.

steps.x: C. Bariatric surgery. Surgery: BMI >35 with recent-onset T2DM, or >40 without comorbidities, or first-line if >50.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man with a BMI of 54 kg/m² has hypertension and knee osteoarthritis. He is motivated, has no psychiatric illness and is fit for anaesthesia. He asks what the most effective treatment for his weight would be. His BP is 146/90 mmHg and his HbA1c is 45 mmol/mol.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Bariatric surgery is a first-line option when BMI is above 50.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
BMI over 50 in a fit, motivated man.

elim: Very unlikely to be enough at a BMI above 50.
At BMI above 50, surgery is first-line rather than drug treatment.
Gives modest weight loss; inadequate at this BMI.
Not a definitive treatment; weight is usually regained.

steps.x: A. Bariatric surgery. BMI >50: bariatric surgery is first-line.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with a BMI of 37 kg/m² attends her GP because she plans to start trying for a baby in 3 months. She has no medical history, takes no medication and does not smoke. Her BP is 126/80 mmHg. She asks what she should take before and during pregnancy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Folic acid 400 mcg now, then aspirin from 12 weeks
questions.e: BMI >25: folic acid 400 mcg from ≥1 month pre-conception to the end of the first trimester; BMI >35: low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks to delivery.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: trying for a baby in 3 months
steps.x: BMI above 35 and planning pregnancy: two separate thresholds apply.

elim: Aspirin starts at 12 weeks, and she also needs folic acid.
Must start at least 1 month before conception.
Only with additional VTE risk factors.
Obesity increases neural tube defect and pre-eclampsia risk.

steps.x: B. Folic acid 400 mcg now, then aspirin from 12 weeks. BMI >25 → folic acid 400 mcg; BMI >35 → aspirin from 12 weeks.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman is 16 weeks pregnant. Her BMI is 32 kg/m². She is heterozygous for factor V Leiden and has smoked 15 cigarettes a day for 20 years (15 pack-years). She has no previous VTE. Her BP is 122/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate thromboprophylaxis?
o: LMWH from 28 weeks to 6 weeks postpartum
questions.e: BMI >30 plus heterozygous factor V Leiden plus a 15 pack-year smoking history warrants LMWH from 28 weeks to 6 weeks postpartum.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate thromboprophylaxis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Three VTE risk factors in pregnancy.

elim: Aspirin reduces pre-eclampsia risk, not VTE risk.
Too short for her combination of risk factors.
Three risk factors put her at substantial VTE risk.
Teratogenic and not used for prophylaxis.

steps.x: C. LMWH from 28 weeks to 6 weeks postpartum. Obesity + factor V Leiden + smoking → LMWH 28 weeks to 6 weeks postpartum.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with a BMI that has fallen from 36 to 31 kg/m² over a year with orlistat and a behavioural programme is reviewed. He feels much better. He has hypertension controlled on ramipril. He asks whether he can now be discharged from follow-up.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
questions.e: Long-term obesity care involves regular monitoring and relapse prevention.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate long-term management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Successful loss, but obesity is chronic.

elim: He is losing weight and BMI is now 31.
Weight regain is common without ongoing support.
Not an appropriate change.
Removes relapse prevention.

steps.x: D. Regular monitoring and relapse prevention. Obesity is chronic: monitor and prevent relapse.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has a BMI of 34 kg/m² and a waist circumference of 116 cm, with most fat carried around his abdomen. His fasting insulin is high and his fasting glucose is 6.5 mmol/L. A student asks why central fat in particular causes insulin resistance.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
questions.e: Visceral adiposity reduces adiponectin, causes leptin resistance and raises TNF-alpha and IL-6, driving insulin resistance.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Central fat with high insulin and borderline glucose = insulin resistance.

elim: The mechanism of type 1 diabetes.
Causes insulin resistance in acromegaly, not obesity.
Adiponectin is reduced in visceral obesity, and it improves insulin sensitivity.
Not the mechanism of insulin resistance.

steps.x: A. Adipokine dysregulation from visceral fat. Visceral fat → adipokine dysregulation → insulin resistance.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman with a BMI of 36 kg/m² and type 2 diabetes starts semaglutide injections. After 8 weeks she says she feels full sooner and has less appetite, and has lost 4 kg. Her glucose has improved without any hypoglycaemia.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of these effects?
o: Incretin action slowing gastric emptying and reducing appetite
Inhibition of SGLT2 in the kidney
questions.e: GLP-1 mimetics mimic incretins: glucose-dependent insulin secretion, glucagon suppression, slowed gastric emptying and central appetite reduction.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of these effects? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Early satiety and no hypoglycaemia: glucose-dependent action.

elim: The action of orlistat.
The action of dapagliflozin.
The action of sulfonylureas, which cause hypoglycaemia.
Not a mechanism of GLP-1 mimetics.

steps.x: A. Incretin action slowing gastric emptying and reducing appetite. GLP-1: glucose-dependent insulin, less glucagon, slower emptying, less appetite.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man with a BMI of 31 kg/m² and hypertension starts a weight-loss tablet. After a takeaway meal he develops urgency and oily, foul-smelling stools that float. He has no abdominal pain or weight loss beyond what he expected.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the drug?
